title: Unit testing and designing for extensibility
problem: A rate limiter reads the system clock and a global metrics singleton, so the test for its expiry has to sleep for sixty seconds.
summary: Unit tests check one behaviour in isolation using test doubles (dummy, stub, fake, mock, spy). Testable design injects collaborators, time and randomness and keeps logic pure; the same seams let new behaviour arrive as new implementations and let APIs evolve additively.
catTip: To test whether I meow at 6 a.m., inject a FakeClock and advance it. Do not wait until dawn. I am the fake: same interface as a real cat, far simpler.

recall.q: A class calls System.currentTimeMillis() to expire entries, and the test for expiry sleeps for a minute. What design change fixes this, and which kind of test double do you use?
recall.a: Inject a java.time.Clock through the constructor and read time from it. In the test pass a fake clock, a small working Clock subclass with an advance method, so the test moves time forward instantly. A fake gives real behaviour without infrastructure; a stub would only return canned instants.

guide.breaks: Code that reaches for the real clock, real databases and global singletons can only be tested slowly and end to end, so bugs are found late and refactoring is feared.
guide.tradeoffs: Every seam is an interface and a double to maintain, and tests that mock every interaction become a second copy of the implementation that breaks on every refactor.
guide.explainSimply: A unit test tries one small part of a program on its own, with the slow or unpredictable bits swapped for stand-ins, the way a film uses a stunt double for a dangerous scene. Design that allows the swap also allows new features to be added without touching what already works.
guide.hint: Think about what the class reaches for on its own, and what it could be handed instead.

meow: Arrange: fake clock, empty bowl. Act: advance to 6 a.m. Assert: meow emitted exactly once. Test passes, purr.

quiz.prompt: In a test, an in-memory repository stores and returns orders with real behaviour but no database. Which test double is it?
quiz.explanation: A fake is a working, simplified implementation. A stub only returns canned answers for the calls the test scripts, and a mock verifies that expected calls were made; neither behaves like a real repository across many tests.

quiz.prompt: Code calls System.currentTimeMillis() inside its expiry logic, and the test for 'entries expire after 60 s' sleeps for 61 seconds. What is the best fix?
options: Shorten the window to 1 ms in a test configuration
Inject a Clock through the constructor and advance a fake clock in the test
Use a static-mocking library to intercept System.currentTimeMillis()
Run the slow test only in the nightly build
quiz.explanation: Injecting the clock removes the hidden dependency, makes the test instant and deterministic, and matches the purpose java.time.Clock was designed for. Static mocking works, but leaves the design dependent on a global so that every future test pays the same price.

cards.q: What is the difference between a mock and a stub, in terms of what the test verifies?
cards.a: A stub supplies canned answers and the test then checks state (the order is paid). A mock is given expectations about which calls will happen and the test asks it to verify them, checking behaviour. Use mocks only when the interaction itself is the requirement.

cards.q: How do you remove a public method from a widely used class without breaking callers overnight?
cards.a: Add the replacement first (an additive change), mark the old method @Deprecated with since and forRemoval and point at the replacement, give callers a release to migrate, then delete it. Never change the meaning of the existing method in place.
